Imagine a single leaf on a plant. Most leaves are one solid color — green. But sometimes, you come across a leaf that has patches of white, streaks of yellow, or blotches of cream sitting right alongside the green, all on the same leaf. That leaf isn't diseased (not always, anyway). It's displaying variegation.

Variegation is the quality or state of having two or more distinct colors appearing together on a single surface or organism — typically in the form of patches, streaks, spots, blotches, or bands. It is the word you use to describe that beautiful, multi-toned patchwork you see on certain plants, animals, minerals, or fabrics.

Think of it this way: if something is uniformly one color, there is no variegation. The moment you have irregular zones of different colors coexisting on one thing, you have variegation.

To understand the noun fully, it helps to see the whole family:

  • Variegate (verb) — to make something display multiple colors or to mark it with patches of different colors. "Nature variegated the leaf with white and green."
  • Variegated (adjective) — the describing word. A variegated plant, a variegated marble floor, variegated yarn.
  • Variegation (noun) — the state, quality, or result of being variegated. This is the abstract concept itself. "The variegation of the leaf was striking."
Where You'll Encounter This Word Most

1. In Plants (The Most Common Use)

This is the word's home territory. In botany, variegation refers to the appearance of multiple colors — most often green alongside white, yellow, cream, silver, or pink — in the leaves, stems, or occasionally the fruit of a plant.

Examples of famously variegated plants:

  • Monstera deliciosa 'Albo' — a houseplant with leaves that are half white, half green
  • Pothos 'Golden' — green leaves streaked with golden yellow
  • Caladium — tropical plants with leaves that can be white, red, pink, and green all at once
  • Hostas — garden plants known for their wide, strikingly two-toned leaves

Variegation is so prized in the plant world that variegated versions of common plants often sell for far more money than their plain green counterparts. A single variegated leaf cutting can be worth hundreds of dollars.

2. In Animals

Many animals display natural variegation — multiple colors appearing in patches or bands on their skin, coat, feathers, or shells. A tortoiseshell cat, a koi fish with orange and white patches, a butterfly wing with its complex zones of color — all of these are examples of variegation in nature.

3. In Minerals and Rocks

Many gemstones and rocks are celebrated for their variegation. Malachite (green with darker green swirls), agate (bands of different earthy colors), and jasper are prime examples. The irregular, naturally occurring color patterns within a single stone are its variegation.

4. In Textiles and Yarn

A ball of variegated yarn contains multiple colors — sometimes gradually shifting from red to orange to yellow, sometimes alternating in blocks. When knitted or woven, it produces fabric with natural color variety without the maker having to change threads. The term "variegated yarn" is widely used in knitting and weaving communities.

5. In General, Figurative Use

Variegation can be used more broadly to describe diversity or variety of any kind — not just color. You might read something like:

"The cultural variegation of the city made it endlessly fascinating."

Here it means the rich mix of different cultures, much like patches of different colors on a leaf. This is a more literary, figurative use — a step removed from the literal color-based meaning — but it is accepted and common in formal writing.
Why Does Variegation Happen in Plants? (The Causes)

Since plants are where you'll encounter this word most, it's worth knowing why variegation occurs. There are several causes, and the cause matters because it tells you whether the variegation is stable or unstable.

1. Chimeral Variegation (the most common type)

A plant is made up of millions of cells. In chimeral variegation, some of those cells contain chlorophyll (the green pigment) and some do not — due to a genetic difference between the two populations of cells. The cells without chlorophyll appear white or yellow. These two types of cells grow side by side, producing the patchy two-toned appearance. This is the type of variegation seen in most popular houseplants.

This type is generally stable — the plant will reliably pass on its variegation.

2. Plastid Mutation Variegation

Inside plant cells are structures called plastids, which produce and hold chlorophyll. If a mutation occurs in the plastids, some cells end up without working chlorophyll-producing plastids, and those areas appear white or pale. This type can be unstable, meaning the plant may revert to full green or become entirely white (which is fatal for a plant, since it needs chlorophyll to photosynthesize and make food).

3. Viral Variegation

Some plant viruses disrupt normal chlorophyll production in certain cells, creating patchy, irregular coloration. This kind of variegation is caused by disease and is generally not desirable — it can weaken the plant. Interestingly, some of history's most celebrated variegated tulips (like the famous 17th-century "broken tulips" of the Dutch Golden Age) were later discovered to be variegated due to a virus.

4. Reflective or Blister Variegation

In some plants, tiny air pockets form between layers of leaf cells. These pockets reflect light differently from the surrounding tissue, giving parts of the leaf a silvery, pale, or metallic appearance. This isn't a color pigment difference — it's a structural optical effect. Many begonias display this type.

5. Pattern-Gene Variegation

Some plants are genetically programmed to produce specific, predictable color patterns. This isn't random or caused by a mutation — it's simply how the plant's DNA instructs it to grow. Caladiums are a great example: their elaborate leaf patterns are a normal, stable genetic feature of the plant.
An Important Distinction: Stable vs. Unstable Variegation

This is a practical concept that comes up whenever variegation is discussed seriously.

  • Stable variegation means the plant will consistently produce variegated leaves, and cuttings will also be variegated. This is what collectors want.
  • Unstable variegation means the plant may suddenly produce all-green leaves (called reverting) or, in mutation-based cases, all-white leaves. All-green reverts are common because green cells grow faster and more vigorously (they have more energy from photosynthesis), and they can eventually outcompete the variegated cells. Gardeners who want to preserve variegation must prune away any fully green growth that appears.

Not all variegation looks the same. Here are the common visual patterns it can take:

  • Sectoral — one half or large section of a leaf is one color, the other section is another. Very dramatic.
  • Mottled / Marbled — irregular, unpredictable splashes and blotches of two or more colors mixed together.
  • Marginal — a border or edge of one color (often white or yellow) running around the rim of a leaf, with the center being a different color (often green).
  • Striped / Streaked — thin lines or streaks of a contrasting color running through the leaf.
  • Speckled / Flecked — tiny dots or specks of a different color scattered across the surface.

1. "The nursery specialized in rare plants, and the stunning variegation on the monstera leaves drew immediate attention from every customer who walked in."
  2. "Geologists admired the natural variegation of the agate specimen — its concentric bands of red, white, and brown were a record of millions of years of mineral deposits."
  3. "The weaver chose variegated thread specifically to add depth and visual interest to the tapestry without having to switch colors manually."
  4. "The plant collector worried when she noticed her variegated pothos pushing out fully green leaves — reverting plants lose their variegation, and this one seemed to be heading in that direction."
  5. "The poet's work was celebrated for its variegation — its moods shifted from grief to joy to irony, sometimes within a single stanza." (figurative use)

Variegation is the quality or state of having two or more distinct colors appearing together on a single surface or organism — in patches, streaks, or irregular zones — and while it occurs across nature, textiles, and minerals, it is most precisely and commonly used to describe the multi-colored patterning seen on plant leaves and other living things.
